Not through an angel, not through a ritual, not through the passage of time. He himself will do it. The intimacy of this act — a Father wiping tears from his children’s faces — is the final word on the relationship between God and his people. All the tears of the tribulation, all the tears of history, all the tears of the church across all ages — wiped away by the hand of God himself.

verseByVerse.quote: After this I looked, and behold, a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, clothed in white robes, with palm branches in their hands, and crying out with a loud voice, "Salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The four-fold description — nation, tribe, people, language — is Revelation’s fullest formula for the totality of humanity, appearing here and in 5:9; 11:9; 13:7; 14:6; 17:15. Every human ethnic and linguistic category is included. The palm branches recall the festival of Tabernacles (Sukkot), the great harvest festival of Israel that was also eschatological in orientation — Zechariah 14 describes all nations coming to Jerusalem to celebrate Tabernacles in the new age. Standing before the throne with palms is the fulfilment of Tabernacles: the harvest of the nations has come in, the feast has begun.

“Salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!” is not a declaration about the process of salvation but a declaration of its ownership. Salvation is not a product that God and the Lamb make available and humans then choose — it belongs to them, in the same way that glory and honor and power belong to the one on the throne (4:11). The acclamation of the redeemed is the acclamation of those who understand that they are there entirely because of grace, and whose only response is to return all the credit to its source.

verseByVerse.quote: And all the angels were standing around the throne and around the elders and the four living creatures, and they fell on their faces before the throne and worshiped God, saying, "Amen! Blessing and glory and wisdom and thanksgiving and honor and power and might be to our God forever and ever! Amen."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angelic response to the multitude’s acclamation is another seven-fold doxology — matching the seven-fold doxology of 5:12 ascribed to the Lamb. Seven attributes of God proclaimed by the angels who have no personal experience of salvation but who worship the God who saves. The redeemed worship because they have been saved; the angels worship because they witness what salvation is.

The double “Amen” — beginning and ending the doxology — is the liturgical seal of affirmation. In Jewish worship, “Amen” was the congregation’s response to prayer (1 Chronicles 16:36; Nehemiah 8:6). In Revelation, it is heaven’s seal on the truth of what has just been declared. The angels’ “Amen” is the cosmic ratification of the redeemed community’s cry.

verseByVerse.quote: Then one of the elders addressed me, saying, "Who are these, clothed in white robes, and from where have they come?" I said to him, "Sir, you know." And he said to me, "These are the ones coming out of the great tribulation. They have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The elder’s question is pedagogical — he knows the answer and wants John (and through John, the church) to receive it as instruction, not merely information. The question “from where have they come?” is the question every suffering believer eventually asks about the great multitude: How did they get there? What qualified them to stand? The answer is not “they were righteous enough” or “they endured well enough” — it is “they washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.”

“Coming out of the great tribulation” has been understood as: (a) emerging from the specific seven-year tribulation in dispensational reading, (b) emerging from the entire period of the church’s tribulation across history (the amillennial reading, noting that “tribulation” is what Jesus promised all his followers — John 16:33 — and what characterizes the whole church age). The crucial point is that they come out of it — they are not destroyed by it. The tribulation they endured has not had the final word. The last word is white robes.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore they are before the throne of God, and serve him day and night in his temple; and he who sits on the throne will shelter them with his presence. They shall hunger no more, neither thirst anymore; the sun shall not strike them, nor any scorching heat. For the Lamb in the midst of the throne will be their shepherd, and he will guide them to springs of living water, and God will wipe away every tear from their eyes."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The five promises of the final state reverse the five sufferings of the tribulation: the exclusion from God’s presence is reversed by sheltering in his presence; the hunger is reversed by the Lamb’s provision; the thirst is reversed by springs of living water; the scorching heat is reversed by his shelter; and the tears — the accumulated tears of all the suffering — are wiped away by the hand of God himself. These are not abstract theological propositions; they are the specific reversal of specific suffering.

The Shepherd-Lamb is the final image of the chapter and one of the most profound christological images in Revelation. The one who was himself slaughtered is now the shepherd who leads to springs of living water. Jesus’ self-identification as the Good Shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11) is fulfilled: the laying down of his life is precisely what qualifies him to be the eternal shepherd. He leads to living water because he himself is the source of living water (John 4:10; 7:37–38; Revelation 22:1). And God himself wipes the tears — the word “wipe away” is the word used for erasing writing from a tablet, for blotting out completely. The tears are not merely comforted; they are erased.

8.title: The Seventh Seal and the First Four Trumpets
8.overview:
The seventh seal does not release a horseman or a cosmic catastrophe. It releases silence. “When the Lamb opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour.” After the unceasing worship of chapters 4–7, after the thunder and lightning of the throne room, after the cries of the martyrs and the acclamation of the great multitude — silence. Heaven holds its breath. The silence of the seventh seal is more terrifying than any of the sounds that preceded it, because it signals that something of ultimate gravity is about to happen.

Out of the silence, seven trumpets are given to seven angels. Before the trumpets sound, another angel offers incense before the altar — and the prayers of the saints rise with the incense before God. This is the answer to the martyrs’ prayer of 6:10 (“How long, O Lord?”): the prayers of God’s people are not lost. They have been gathered. They are being presented before the throne. And now fire from the altar is thrown to the earth — the prayers of the saints become the fire of divine judgment.

The trumpets follow the pattern of the Exodus plagues, but escalated. Hail, fire, blood — the first trumpet echoes the seventh plague of Egypt. The sea turning to blood — the second trumpet echoes the first plague. Darkness — the fourth trumpet echoes the ninth plague. The Exodus pattern is deliberate: the God who judged Egypt to liberate his people is now judging the new Egypt (Rome, Babylon) to liberate the new Israel (the church). The judgments of Revelation are not arbitrary cruelties; they are the exodus of the new covenant people on a cosmic scale.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The Seventh Seal and the Golden Censer
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The half-hour silence is the most dramatic pause in all of Revelation. Heaven, which has been filled with the sound of worship and thunder and the voices of angels and the living creatures, falls completely silent. The effect is cinematic — the withdrawal of all sound is more arresting than any sound. The silence of the seventh seal is the silence of reverent anticipation before the final sequence of judgments, the silence of a courtroom before the judge speaks.

Into this silence come seven angels who stand before God — the “seven angels who stand before God” echoes both Tobit 12:15 (the angel Raphael identifies himself as one of the seven holy angels who present the prayers of the holy ones) and the seven archangels of Jewish tradition (Michael, Gabriel, Raphael, and four others). They are given seven trumpets — the instruments of divine announcement in Israel’s worship (Numbers 10) and warfare (Joshua 6). The Jericho pattern is in view: the walls fall not at human assault but at the sound of the divine trumpet.

Before the trumpets sound, another angel with a golden censer stands at the altar. He is given much incense to offer with the prayers of all the saints on the golden altar before the throne. This is the incense-priest of the heavenly temple, and his ministry makes visible what is invisible: the prayers of God’s people rise before God. Every prayer prayed in suffering and darkness and apparent unanswer has been preserved, gathered, offered. The smoke of the incense rises. Then the angel takes the censer, fills it with fire from the altar, and throws it to the earth. Thunder, rumblings, flashes of lightning, an earthquake. The prayers of the saints become the fire of judgment.
verseByVerse.theology:
The altar-fire thrown to earth from the prayers of the saints is one of Revelation’s most startling images of the power of prayer. The prayers of suffering believers are not merely heard; they are instrumentally active in the events of history. The judgments that follow in the trumpet series are not God’s arbitrary decisions unrelated to the church’s cry — they are the divine response to the accumulated intercession of his people. This does not make God a vending machine who responds to sufficient prayer; it demonstrates that God has woven the prayers of his people into the very fabric of how he governs history.

The silence of half an hour is theologically significant. In the regular liturgy of the Jerusalem temple, the offering of incense was the moment of deepest silence — the congregation stood outside in silence while the priest burned incense in the Holy Place. The half-hour silence of Revelation 8 places the entire sequence of the seven trumpets in the context of the heavenly liturgy. History is liturgical; its events unfold in the context of heavenly worship and priestly intercession.
verseByVerse.examples:
The image of the prayers of the saints gathered in the golden bowls (5:8) and now rising as incense before the altar is the answer to every believer who has wondered whether their prayers accomplish anything. The widow who prays for her persecutors, the martyr who cries “How long?” before dying, the faithful remnant who intercedes for the church’s renewal — every prayer is in those bowls. Not one has been lost. God keeps them. And the fire that falls on the earth comes from the altar where those prayers were offered.

The silence of heaven before judgment is also a pattern for the church’s approach to the most solemn realities. There is a time for the exuberance of praise (chapters 4–5) and a time for the silence of awe. The church that never falls silent before God — that treats every moment of worship as an opportunity for performance or emotional expression — has lost something that heaven itself practices.

verseByVerse.quote: When the Lamb opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour. Then I saw the seven angels who stand before God, and seven trumpets were given to them. And another angel came and stood at the altar with a golden censer, and he was given much incense to offer with the prayers of all the saints on the golden altar before the throne, and the smoke of the incense, with the prayers of the saints, rose before God from the hand of the angel. Then the angel took the censer and filled it with fire from the altar and threw it on the earth, and there were peals of thunder, rumblings, flashes of lightning, and an earthquake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The silence for “about half an hour” is the only temporal measurement in the throne room scenes. Its specificity makes it feel experiential — this is not a symbolic number but an actual duration, enough time to feel the weight of the silence. The seven angels who “stand before God” are the archangels of Jewish tradition, the highest order of heavenly beings, now assigned the solemn task of sounding the trumpets that will shake the earth.

The golden altar before the throne is the heavenly counterpart of the altar of incense in the Jerusalem temple (Exodus 30:1–10). The incense offered there was the symbol of prayer ascending to God (Psalm 141:2; Luke 1:10). The “prayers of all the saints” — not just the martyrs of 6:9, but all the saints across all time — are gathered with the incense. The theological claim is staggering: the small, faltering, sometimes barely-articulate prayers of ordinary believers are gathered before the throne of the Almighty and offered as incense that pleases him.

The fire thrown from the altar to the earth reverses the direction of incense: incense rises (prayer ascending to God); fire falls (judgment descending from God). The same altar that receives the prayers of the saints is the source of the fire that answers them. This is not a cold, mechanical divine justice; it is the justice that flows from the intimacy of the divine-human relationship. The Judge who hears the cries acts.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The first four trumpets follow in quick succession, each affecting one of the four domains of the created order: the earth, the sea, the fresh waters, and the heavens. In each case, a third is affected — a substantial but bounded proportion. The pattern of the Exodus plagues runs throughout: hail and fire (first trumpet, echoing the seventh plague), blood (second trumpet, echoing the first plague), the star Wormwood turning the waters bitter (third trumpet, echoing the waters turning bitter in Exodus 15:23), and darkness (fourth trumpet, echoing the ninth plague). God is demonstrating, for the new exodus, the same sovereign power over creation that he demonstrated in Egypt.

The limitation of a third in each judgment is theologically significant. The judgments are real and severe — a third of the earth, a third of the sea, a third of the rivers, a third of the sun, moon, and stars. But two-thirds remain. These are not the final judgment; they are the penultimate judgments — severe enough to call the world to repentance, bounded enough to leave room for it. This is the mercy that runs through the wrath of Revelation: judgment is never total until the very end, because the space for repentance is preserved within it.

The chapter ends with a solitary eagle flying in midheaven, crying “Woe, woe, woe to those who dwell on the earth, at the blasts of the other three trumpets that the three angels are about to blow!” The eagle’s cry marks the transition from the first four trumpets (which affect the physical creation) to the final three trumpets (which directly affect humanity). The three woes correspond to the fifth, sixth, and seventh trumpets. The escalation is deliberate: what has come is severe; what is coming is worse.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Exodus typology of the trumpets carries a profound theological message: the God who acts in Revelation is the same God who acted in Egypt. He is not a new God with a new character, revealed for the first time in the New Testament as a God of judgment. He is the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the God who hardened Pharaoh’s heart and brought ten plagues on Egypt and parted the Red Sea — and he is acting again in the same pattern for the same purpose: the liberation of his people from bondage to an empire that refuses to release them.

The bounded nature of the trumpet judgments — a third, not all — reflects the distinction in Reformed theology between common grace and final judgment. God restrains the full expression of his wrath throughout history, partly for the sake of the elect who have not yet come to faith (2 Peter 3:9: “the Lord is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance”) and partly as an expression of his own patience and long-suffering. The full wrath is reserved for the final bowls.
verseByVerse.examples:
The ecological dimensions of the trumpet judgments — the earth burned, the sea corrupted, the rivers poisoned, the sky darkened — speak with surprising contemporary relevance. The creation that humanity has been given to tend and keep (Genesis 2:15) groans under the weight of human sin and divine judgment simultaneously. Revelation does not invite us to be indifferent to the created order on the grounds that it will all be burned up anyway — it shows us that the corruption of creation is itself a form of divine judgment, a sign that something has gone deeply wrong.

The eagle’s warning cry — “Woe, woe, woe” — is a summons to sobriety. The church in every age lives between the trumpets that have already sounded and the woes that are yet to come. This is not a call to despair but to alertness — the same alertness commended in the letters to Sardis and Laodicea. Those who hear the eagle’s cry and take it seriously will not be caught asleep when the final woes arrive.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the seven angels who had the seven trumpets prepared to blow them. The first angel blew his trumpet, and there followed hail and fire, mixed with blood, and these were thrown upon the earth. And a third of the earth was burned up, and a third of the trees were burned up, and all green grass was burned up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hail, fire, and blood together echo the seventh plague of Egypt (Exodus 9:22–26) but intensified: in Egypt, hail and fire struck Goshen’s fields; here a third of the entire earth is burned. The scope is cosmic, not local. The trees and the green grass suggest the destruction of the food supply — a form of the famine judgment already seen in the third seal (6:5–6), now played out on a landscape scale.

The “all green grass was burned up” may seem to contradict 9:4 where the locusts are told not to harm the grass. The contradiction is one of the clues that the trumpet series is not strictly sequential chronologically — the visions are successive literary pictures, each complete in itself, not a moment-by-moment timeline. What all green grass being burned up communicates is the thoroughness of the judgment within its domain, not a literal global scorching that removes all vegetation before the next scene begins.

verseByVerse.quote: The second angel blew his trumpet, and something like a great mountain, burning with fire, was thrown into the sea, and a third of the sea became blood. A third of the living creatures in the sea died, and a third of the ships were destroyed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The burning mountain cast into the sea echoes Jeremiah 51:25, where Babylon is called a “destroying mountain” that God will make “a burnt mountain.” To a first-century Roman audience, the sea turning to blood would recall both the first Exodus plague (Exodus 7:20–21) and the catastrophic volcanic eruption of Vesuvius in AD 79, which turned the Mediterranean red with ash and debris and killed fish and destroyed ships along the Bay of Naples. The preterist reading sees a direct allusion; the idealist reading sees a recurring pattern of divine judgment on the sea-powers that traffic in the goods of Babylon (chapter 18).

The destruction of ships is an economic judgment — the trade routes that sustained the empire’s wealth are disrupted. Revelation consistently targets the economic structures of Babylon (chapters 17–18), not merely its military power. The judgment works by dismantling what the empire depends on.

verseByVerse.quote: The third angel blew his trumpet, and a great star fell from heaven, blazing like a torch, and it fell on a third of the rivers and on the springs of water. The name of the star is Wormwood. A third of the waters became wormwood, and many people died from the water, because it had been made bitter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wormwood (apsinthos) is a bitter plant used in the Old Testament as a metaphor for divine judgment and the consequences of apostasy (Jeremiah 9:15; 23:15; Lamentations 3:15, 19; Amos 5:7). The star named Wormwood falling on the fresh waters — the rivers and springs that sustain life inland — is the poisoning of the sources of life. Where the second trumpet targeted the salt water (commerce and empire), the third targets the fresh water (the sustenance of ordinary human life).

A great star blazing like a torch falling from heaven may evoke Isaiah 14:12 — “How you are fallen from heaven, O Day Star, son of Dawn!” — the fall of Babylon described as the fall of a heavenly star. The idealist reading sees every judgment on the water supply as an instance of this pattern: the powers that corrupt and pollute the sources of life are themselves judged through that corruption. The bitter water is both a judgment and a symptom.

verseByVerse.quote: The fourth angel blew his trumpet, and a third of the sun was struck, and a third of the moon, and a third of the stars, so that a third of their light might be darkened, and a third of the day might be kept from shining, and likewise a third of the night. Then I looked, and I heard an eagle crying with a loud voice as it flew directly overhead, "Woe, woe, woe to those who dwell on the earth, at the blasts of the other three trumpets that the three angels are about to blow!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The darkening of a third of the sun, moon, and stars echoes the ninth plague of Egypt (Exodus 10:21–23) and the Day of the LORD imagery of Joel 2:10–11 and Amos 8:9. In the Old Testament, the lights of heaven are the fixed reference points of creation — the greater and lesser lights that “rule” day and night (Genesis 1:16). Their partial darkening signals the destabilization of the created order’s most fundamental structures. The world is losing its orientation.

The eagle flying in midheaven (“directly overhead” — the zenith point where a herald would be most visible) crying “Woe, woe, woe” is a triple woe corresponding to the three remaining trumpets. In the Old Testament, the eagle was associated with swift judgment (Deuteronomy 28:49; Jeremiah 48:40; Hosea 8:1). The triple repetition of “woe” echoes the triple holiness of 4:8 — as holiness is thrice declared, so woe is thrice announced. The symmetry is not accidental.

9.title: The Fifth and Sixth Trumpets: The Demonic and the Deadly
9.overview:
Chapter 9 is among the most vivid and terrifying in Revelation. The fifth trumpet releases demonic locusts from the abyss — creatures drawn from Joel 2 and shaped like scorpions, with the faces of humans and the hair of women and the teeth of lions. The sixth trumpet releases four angels bound at the great Euphrates river, who command an army of two hundred million mounted troops. The devastation escalates from the bounded third of the earlier trumpets to something more comprehensive and more personal: now humanity itself is directly targeted.

The two woe-trumpets of chapter 9 share a common theme: demonic power unleashed. The fifth trumpet releases the army of the abyss, led by “the angel of the bottomless pit” whose name in Hebrew is Abaddon and in Greek Apollyon — “Destroyer.” The sixth releases an army from beyond the Euphrates — the frontier from which Israel’s ancient enemies (Assyria, Babylon) had always come. The locust-army of the fifth trumpet torments but does not kill; the cavalry of the sixth kills a third of humanity. The escalation is purposeful: God is turning up the pressure on a world that refuses to repent.

The chapter’s most sobering verse is its final one: “The rest of mankind, who were not killed by these plagues, did not repent.” The purpose of the trumpet judgments — like the purpose of the Exodus plagues — was to break the hardness of heart that keeps humanity from turning to God. Pharaoh’s hardness repeated in every generation: even faced with the unmistakable signs of divine judgment, even watching a third of their companions die, the survivors “did not repent of the works of their hands nor give up worshiping demons.” The judgment does not automatically produce repentance; only grace can break what judgment cannot.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Fifth Trumpet: The Locusts from the Abyss
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
A star falls from heaven to earth — this time not a literal star but a being, since “he was given the key to the shaft of the bottomless pit.” The fallen star is most likely a fallen angel (the language of “falling from heaven” is used of Satan in Isaiah 14:12 and Luke 10:18) given temporary authority to open the abyss. The abyss — abyssos — is the realm of the demonic dead (Luke 8:31; Romans 10:7), the prison of rebellious spirits (2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6), and in Revelation the dwelling of the beast (11:7; 17:8) and the binding place of Satan (20:1–3).

When the shaft is opened, smoke pours out like a great furnace, darkening the sun and air. From the smoke emerge locusts — but not ordinary locusts. They are composite creatures: shaped like warhorses, wearing crowns like gold, with human faces and women’s hair and lion’s teeth and scorpion’s tails and the sound of chariots. Joel 2:4–5 describes the locust army of the Day of the LORD as like war horses; John takes Joel’s metaphor and makes it literal in the symbolic world of the vision. These are demonic forces wearing the shape of natural plague to reveal the supernatural reality behind what the world calls ordinary catastrophe.

The locusts are given carefully defined limits: they may not harm the grass, trees, or any green plant (the domain of the first trumpet’s judgment). They may only harm people who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads. Their torture lasts five months — the lifespan of a locust, a bounded season. People will want to die and cannot. The limitation is mercy within judgment: even the unleashing of demonic torment is bounded by the sovereign will of the Lamb.
verseByVerse.theology:
The demonic army of the fifth trumpet raises the question of how demonic power operates within divine sovereignty. Revelation’s consistent answer is that demonic powers are real, powerful, and destructive — but they operate within limits set by God. They are given authority (“they were given power”), they are given a season (“five months”), they are given boundaries (“not to harm the grass”; “those who have the seal of God” are protected). Satan and his forces are not free agents running loose in God’s universe; they are bound agents, whose very destructiveness is enlisted in the divine governance of history.

The protection of the sealed (those with the seal of God on their foreheads) from the locust-torment is the practical outworking of the sealing in chapter 7. The seal is not merely a metaphysical status — it has real protective force in the spiritual realm. This does not mean that believers are exempt from all suffering; the martyrs of 6:9–11 are plainly not. But the specific torment of the demonic locusts — the spiritual anguish of those who belong to the kingdom of darkness — does not touch those who belong to the kingdom of light.
verseByVerse.examples:
The description of people seeking death and not finding it (v. 6) is one of the most psychologically acute passages in Revelation. It describes the condition of those so tormented by the consequences of their rejection of God that death would be a relief — and even death is not available to them. The judgment is not quick; it is prolonged. This is the condition of those who have spent their lives refusing the only one who can give them rest (Matthew 11:28), now confronted with restlessness as judgment.

The seal of God protecting the sealed from the locust-torment is the pastoral assurance that runs beneath the horror of chapter 9. However dark the world around the church becomes — however manifest the demonic powers in culture, in persecution, in spiritual warfare — the sealed cannot be destroyed. The locusts see the seal and pass over. The church in the middle of the fifth trumpet is Goshen in the middle of the plagues.

verseByVerse.quote: And the fifth angel blew his trumpet, and I saw a star fallen from heaven to earth, and he was given the key to the shaft of the bottomless pit. He opened the shaft of the bottomless pit, and from the shaft rose smoke like the smoke of a great furnace, and the sun and the air were darkened with the smoke from the shaft.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The star that has “fallen” from heaven is a person, not an astronomical object — the masculine pronoun and the key given to “him” make this clear. The perfect tense “fallen” may suggest a being already in the state of having fallen, a reference to the expulsion of Satan from heaven (12:7–9; Luke 10:18; Isaiah 14:12). This fallen being is given the key — note: given it, not seizing it. Even the opening of the abyss is an authorized act, within the governance of the Lamb.

The smoke from the abyss darkening the sun and air reverses the creation pattern: on the fourth day God made the lights of the heavens to give light to the earth (Genesis 1:14–16); the smoke of the abyss extinguishes that light. The demonic powers are anti-creation forces, bringing darkness where God brought light, chaos where God brought order. The fourth trumpet partially darkened the heavens from above; the fifth darkens the air from below — the encroachment of the abyss on the atmosphere of the living.

verseByVerse.quote: Then from the smoke came locusts on the earth, and they were given power like the power of scorpions of the earth. They were told not to harm the grass of the earth or any green plant or any tree, but only those people who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads. They were allowed to torment them for five months, but not to kill them, and their torment was like the torment of a scorpion when it stings someone. And in those days people will seek death and will not find it. They will long to die, but death will flee from them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The restrictions placed on the locust-demons reveal the structure of divine judgment: real pain, real suffering, but bounded by specific prohibitions and a time limit. They cannot harm the vegetation (the domain of the first trumpet), they cannot harm the sealed, they cannot kill, they are limited to five months. This is not weakness in the demonic forces — it is the restraining hand of the sovereign God, who even in the releasing of demonic powers maintains control of their scope and duration.

The scorpion sting produces intense, prolonged pain that is not immediately lethal — the victim suffers and survives. The spiritual application is the torment of a life lived in rebellion against God: the accumulating consequences of having rejected the one who gives life, now experienced as active suffering without relief. The desire for death that cannot be satisfied echoes Job’s cry (Job 3:21) and Jonah’s (Jonah 4:3, 8) — but those were the cries of righteous men in extreme distress; this is the cry of those whose distress is the direct consequence of their own choices.

verseByVerse.quote: In appearance the locusts were like horses prepared for battle: on their heads were what looked like crowns of gold; their faces were like human faces, their hair like women's hair, and their teeth like lions' teeth; they had breastplates like breastplates of iron, and the noise of their wings was like the noise of many chariots with horses rushing into battle. They have tails and stings like scorpions, and their power to hurt people for five months is in their tails.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The composite description draws on Joel 2:4–5 (locusts like war horses), the Parthian cavalry that terrified the Roman world (long hair, iron-clad), and the mythological creatures of the ancient Near East. No single natural creature has all these features simultaneously — the impossibility of the description signals its symbolic character. This is demonic power as it truly is: a nightmarish combination of beauty (gold crowns, human faces, women’s hair), brute force (iron breastplates, lion’s teeth), and deadly purpose (scorpion’s tails).

The crowns of gold suggest a counterfeit royalty — the demonic powers mimic the true royalty of the Lamb and his people (the same word, stephanoi, used for the crowns of the twenty-four elders in 4:4 and the crown given to the first horseman in 6:2). Everything the adversary offers is a counterfeit of what the Lamb genuinely gives: false crowns, false power, false worship.

verseByVerse.quote: They have as king over them the angel of the bottomless pit. His name in Hebrew is Abaddon, and in Greek he is called Apollyon. The first woe has passed; behold, two woes are still to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abaddon in Hebrew and Apollyon in Greek both mean “Destroyer.” The name appears in the Old Testament as a place — Abaddon is the realm of the dead, synonymous with Sheol (Job 26:6; Proverbs 15:11; Psalm 88:11). Here it is the name of a being — the angelic king of the demonic realm. Some have identified Apollyon with the Greek god Apollo (whose symbol was the locust), suggesting a deliberate counter-imperial jab at the emperor Domitian, who associated himself with Apollo. Whether or not the Apollo connection is intended, the name “Destroyer” defines the demonic agenda without remainder: the adversary’s kingdom is the kingdom of destruction, the antithesis of the Creator whose name is Life.

The announcement “the first woe has passed; behold, two woes are still to come” marks the structural progression. The reader is being told: we are not yet at the end. The demonic torment of the fifth trumpet, as terrible as it is, is not the worst. What follows will be worse. The escalation of Revelation is purposeful: each series (seals, trumpets, bowls) intensifies, each woe exceeds the last, driving toward the climax of the final judgment and the new creation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–21 — The Sixth Trumpet: The Army from the Euphrates
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
A voice from the golden altar before God commands the sixth angel to release four angels bound at the great river Euphrates. The Euphrates was the eastern boundary of the Roman Empire — the frontier beyond which the feared Parthian cavalry waited. For John’s readers, the Euphrates was the boundary between the known world of Rome and the threatening unknown beyond. It was also the boundary of the Promised Land in its maximum extent (Genesis 15:18; Deuteronomy 1:7), and the river beside which Israel had mourned in Babylonian exile (Psalm 137:1). Everything fearful came from beyond the Euphrates.

The four angels released at the Euphrates command an army of two hundred million mounted troops. The army’s horses breathe fire, smoke, and sulfur from their mouths — the three plagues that kill a third of humanity. The image is deliberately excessive: two hundred million is not a literal military count but the symbolic representation of an overwhelming, unstoppable force. The sixth trumpet escalates beyond the fifth: the fifth tortured but did not kill; the sixth kills a third of humanity.

The chapter concludes with the most heartbreaking verse in the trumpet series: “The rest of mankind, who were not killed by these plagues, did not repent of the works of their hands nor give up worshiping demons and idols.” The entire purpose of the trumpet judgments — to call humanity to repentance before the final judgment — is frustrated. Pharaoh’s hardness is the pattern of every age. Judgment, as such, does not produce repentance; only the grace of God can do that. The trumpets judge; only the gospel saves.
verseByVerse.theology:
The voice from the golden altar (v. 13) commands the release of the sixth trumpet judgment. This is the same altar from which the prayers of the saints rose (8:3–5) and from which fire was thrown to the earth. The altar is simultaneously the place of intercession and the place from which judgment proceeds. This is not a contradiction — it is the unity of God’s justice and mercy. The prayers of the saints for justice are answered through the judgments that proceed from the altar. The saints do not pray for revenge; they pray for God’s righteousness to be vindicated. The judgments are the vindication.

The hardening of humanity in vv. 20–21 raises the Reformed doctrine of judicial hardening. God did not create the hardness; the idolatry and wickedness of humanity created it. But God’s judgments, which should soften, instead harden those who have made their choice. This is the mystery of reprobation that Paul discusses in Romans 9–11: God’s patience borne and rejected becomes, in the economy of divine justice, the occasion for final hardening.
verseByVerse.examples:
The non-repentance of the survivors (vv. 20–21) is the pastoral center of chapter 9. It warns against the assumption that sufficient suffering will bring people to faith. It does not. Suffering alone, without the proclamation of the gospel, without the regenerating work of the Spirit, produces not repentance but resentment, numbness, or despair. The church’s ministry in a world of judgment is not to intensify the suffering (God does that without our help) but to proclaim the gospel that alone can break the hardness that judgment cannot.

The specific list of sins from which the survivors do not repent — worshipping demons and idols, murder, sorceries, sexual immorality, theft — is a first-century inventory that maps directly to any contemporary culture. Idolatry takes different forms in different ages (the stock market, social media approval, sexual autonomy, national pride) but its structure is always the same: attributing to a creature the devotion that belongs to the Creator.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the sixth angel blew his trumpet, and I heard a voice from the four horns of the golden altar before God, saying to the sixth angel who had the trumpet, "Release the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates." So the four angels, who had been prepared for the hour, the day, the month, and the year, were released to kill a third of mankind. The number of mounted troops was twice ten thousand times ten thousand; I heard their number.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The four angels bound at the Euphrates have been prepared for a specific moment: “the hour, the day, the month, and the year.” The precision of the divine timing is absolute — to the hour. The forces of judgment do not wander loose through history, striking when opportunity arises. They are bound, held, waiting for the precise moment that God has appointed. This is the sovereignty of God over the timing of history expressed with almost mathematical exactness.

Two hundred million (twice ten thousand times ten thousand) is a number beyond any literal army in human history — the entire human population of the first century was perhaps 200–300 million. The number is symbolic of an overwhelming, humanly irresistible force. In the preterist reading, the Parthian cavalry beyond the Euphrates is in view; in the idealist reading, the demonic army behind every human military force. In either case, the message is: no human power can withstand this army, just as no human power could withstand the army of Pharaoh at the Red Sea — except that Israel was on the other side of the sea, and God fought for them.

verseByVerse.quote: And this is how I saw the horses in my vision and those who rode them: they wore breastplates the color of fire and of sapphire and of sulfur, and the heads of the horses were like lions' heads, and fire and smoke and sulfur came out of their mouths. By these three plagues a third of mankind was killed, by the fire and smoke and sulfur coming out of their mouths. For the power of the horses is in their mouths and in their tails, for their tails are like serpents with heads, and by means of them they wound.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The three-colored breastplates — fire-red, sapphire-blue, sulfur-yellow — correspond to the three plagues that issue from the horses’ mouths: fire, smoke, and sulfur. Sulfur (“brimstone” in older translations) is the divine judgment material par excellence, associated with the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19:24) and recurring throughout Revelation as the substance of the lake of fire (19:20; 20:10; 21:8).

The serpentine tails that wound are a detail that deepens the demonic character of the army: the serpent goes all the way back to the garden, the original instrument of deception and death. The demonic army of the sixth trumpet combines the lion (predatory power, frontal assault) with the serpent (deceptive, striking from behind, venomous). This is how the adversary’s work always operates: both direct and subtle, both overwhelming force and quiet infiltration.

verseByVerse.quote: The rest of mankind, who were not killed by these plagues, did not repent of the works of their hands nor give up worshiping demons and idols of gold and silver and bronze and stone and wood, which cannot see or hear or walk, nor did they repent of their murders or their sorceries or their sexual immorality or their thefts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The catalogue of idolatry — gold, silver, bronze, stone, wood — echoes Daniel 5:4 and 5:23, where Belshazzar and his court praised gods of gold, silver, bronze, iron, wood, and stone at the very feast where the writing appeared on the wall. The inability of idols to see, hear, or walk echoes Psalm 115:4–7 and Isaiah 44:9–20. The irony is deep: people who can see and hear and walk prefer gods who cannot. This is the madness of idolatry that Paul describes in Romans 1:21–23.

The five sins from which the survivors do not repent — idolatry, murder, sorceries (pharmakeia — drug-magic, occult practice), sexual immorality, and theft — are the social consequences of the idolatry that heads the list. Idolatry is not merely a spiritual problem; it deforms the whole moral and social life of those who practice it. The refusal to repent of idolatry means the refusal to repent of the moral destruction that idolatry produces.

10.title: The Angel and the Little Scroll
10.overview:
Chapter 10 is the second great interlude of Revelation — this one inserted between the sixth and seventh trumpets (as chapter 7 was inserted between the sixth and seventh seals). The interlude performs the same function: it pauses the judgment sequence to reorient the reader to the prophetic commission of the church. Before the seventh trumpet sounds and the final woe arrives, John is given a little scroll to eat and recommissioned to prophesy.

A mighty angel descends from heaven clothed with a cloud, with a rainbow over his head, his face like the sun, his legs like pillars of fire — imagery that deliberately echoes the description of Christ in chapter 1. He stands on sea and land (claiming sovereignty over the whole earth), holds a little open scroll, and cries out with a loud voice like a lion’s roar. Seven thunders respond — and John is told not to write what the thunders said. This is the only thing in Revelation that is sealed rather than revealed: some of God’s purposes remain hidden until their time.

John eats the little scroll at the angel’s command. It is sweet in his mouth but bitter in his stomach — an echo of Ezekiel’s commissioning (Ezekiel 2:8–3:3) and Jeremiah’s experience of the word (Jeremiah 15:16). The word of God is sweet to receive — it is the good news of grace, the promise of the kingdom, the comfort of the gospel. But the prophetic task is bitter: to speak God’s word to a world that does not want to hear it, to witness to the truth in the face of hostility, to suffer for the testimony of Jesus. The whole book of Revelation is this little scroll: sweet with the glory of the Lamb, bitter with the suffering of faithful witness.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Angel and the Little Scroll
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The mighty angel of chapter 10 is one of the most majestic figures in Revelation. His description borrows directly from the vision of Christ in chapter 1 (face like the sun, voice like thunder) and from the description of God’s theophany in the Old Testament (cloud, rainbow, pillars of fire). Whether this is Christ himself or a high-ranking angel reflecting the glory of the one he represents is debated — the Reformed consensus tends to see him as a glorious angel, since the book distinguishes between Christ and angels throughout; but the christological imagery is unmistakable. Whatever the identity, the angel’s appearance announces that what is about to happen carries the full weight of divine authority.

The seven thunders that speak after the angel’s lion-roar are a unique feature of this vision. John is about to write what they said — and is told not to. The sealed thunders are a reminder that not everything about God’s governance of history is disclosed. Revelation is an unveiling, but it is not a total disclosure. Some things remain sealed. Deuteronomy 29:29 applies: “The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children forever.” The Christian interpreter must resist the temptation to speculate about the sealed thunders — if God chose not to reveal them, the appropriate response is worship, not curiosity.

The angel’s oath (vv. 5–7) is one of the most solemn moments in the book: he swears by the living Creator that “there will be no more delay.” When the seventh trumpet sounds, the mystery of God will be fulfilled, as he announced to his servants the prophets. The delay is over. The patience of God that has held back judgment for the sake of the elect will be exhausted. The “mystery of God” that will be fulfilled is the redemptive plan announced through the prophets — the new creation, the final kingdom, the consummation of all things in Christ. This is the end of the delay, not the end of hope.

The eating of the scroll completes John’s recommissioning. He must “prophesy again about many peoples and nations and languages and kings.” The book of Revelation does not end at chapter 10; the prophetic task continues. The sweet-and-bitter experience of the scroll is the experience of every Christian who has genuinely engaged with the word of God: the sweetness of the gospel in the heart, the bitterness of the cost of faithful witness in the world. These two are inseparable. You cannot have the sweetness without accepting the bitterness.
verseByVerse.theology:
The sealed thunders raise the question of divine hiddenness alongside divine revelation. Revelation is the great book of divine disclosure — the apokalypsis, the unveiling. But within the unveiling, something remains sealed. God reveals what we need for faithful endurance; he does not reveal everything. This is the epistemological shape of the Christian life: we know enough to trust, not enough to be self-sufficient. “Now I know in part; then I shall know fully” (1 Corinthians 13:12). The humility to leave some things sealed is part of the posture of faith.

The angel’s oath by the Creator recalls God’s oath in Genesis 22 and the oath of Hebrews 6:13–18 — God swearing by himself because there is no higher authority. The solemnity of the oath signals that the declaration of “no more delay” is absolutely certain. God’s patience is real and genuinely prolonged; it is also finite. The interplay between God’s patience (2 Peter 3:9) and God’s decisive action at the appointed time is the rhythm of redemptive history.
verseByVerse.examples:
The bitter-sweet scroll is the experience of every preacher and witness. The gospel is “the sweetness of the knowledge of him” (2 Corinthians 2:14–16) — and it is the aroma of death to those who are perishing. Speaking truth costs. Prophesying “about many peoples and nations and languages and kings” means confronting powers that would prefer silence. John is recommissioned for this task not after the suffering has ended but in the middle of it. The church is always being recommissioned in the middle of the battle.

The sealed thunders are the comfort of every believer facing a question about suffering that has no answer. God knows what the thunders said. He has not revealed it. But he has revealed enough: the Lamb is on the throne, the scroll is being opened, the delay will end, the mystery of God will be fulfilled. That is sufficient for faithful endurance, even without knowing everything. The Christian’s confidence is not in having all the answers but in knowing the one who holds all the answers.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw another mighty angel coming down from heaven, wrapped in a cloud, with a rainbow over his head, and his face was like the sun, and his legs were like pillars of fire. He had a little scroll open in his hand. And he set his right foot on the sea, and his left foot on the land, and called out with a loud voice, like a lion roaring.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The mighty angel’s posture — right foot on the sea, left foot on the land — is a claim to universal sovereignty. He spans the whole earth. The sea and land together constitute the entire created world; by standing on both simultaneously, the angel declares the authority of the message he carries over every domain of creation. This is the prelude to the declaration that there will be no more delay — the whole earth is within the scope of the judgment that is coming.

The little scroll that is “open” in his hand contrasts with the sealed scroll of chapter 5. The great scroll of history was sealed with seven seals; this little scroll is already open. Its contents are immediately available — indeed, John is commanded to eat it. The little scroll is most likely the prophetic commission that John must fulfill: the content of the rest of the book of Revelation, the word he must speak to the nations.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the seven thunders had sounded, I was about to write, but I heard a voice from heaven saying, "Seal up what the seven thunders have said, and do not write it down." And the angel whom I saw standing on the sea and on the land raised his right hand to heaven and swore by him who lives forever and ever, who created heaven and what is in it, the earth and what is in it, and the sea and what is in it, that there would be no more delay, but that in the days of the trumpet call to be sounded by the seventh angel, the mystery of God would be fulfilled, just as he announced to his servants the prophets.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The seven thunders and their sealed content are the most tantalizing feature of this vision. John hears them, understands them (he is about to write them down), and is commanded not to. This is divine self-restraint in revelation: God chooses how much to disclose and when. The interpreter who speculates about the sealed thunders is overriding a divine prohibition. The lesson is the humility of revelation: the book of Revelation reveals much and conceals this. Both the revealing and the concealing are acts of the sovereign God.

The oath formula — raising the right hand to heaven and swearing by the living Creator — echoes Daniel 12:7, where a heavenly figure raises his right hand and swears by the one who lives forever that a time period will come. The angel’s oath parallels Daniel’s oath, positioning the events of Revelation as the fulfillment of Daniel’s prophecies. The “mystery of God” fulfilled at the seventh trumpet is the hidden redemptive plan now brought to completion — the “mystery” of Ephesians 3:3–6 (Jews and Gentiles together in one body in Christ) extended to its cosmic consummation.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the voice that I had heard from heaven spoke to me again, saying, "Go, take the scroll that is open in the hand of the angel who is standing on the sea and on the land." So I went to the angel and told him to give me the little scroll. And he said to me, "Take and eat it; it will make your stomach bitter, but in your mouth it will be sweet as honey." And I took the little scroll from the hand of the angel and ate it. It was sweet as honey in my mouth, but when I had eaten it my stomach was made bitter. And I was told, "You must again prophesy about many peoples and nations and languages and kings."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The eating of the scroll draws on two Old Testament prophetic commissions. Ezekiel was given a scroll written on front and back — words of lamentation, mourning, and woe — and commanded to eat it; it was as sweet as honey in his mouth (Ezekiel 2:8–3:3). Jeremiah “found” God’s words and ate them; they became a joy and the delight of his heart (Jeremiah 15:16) — even though Jeremiah’s prophetic ministry was the most painful in the Old Testament. Eating the word is the classic image of internalizing the prophetic message so completely that it becomes part of you, inseparable from your identity.

The sweetness and bitterness together are not a contradiction but a simultaneity. The gospel is sweet: it announces the victory of the Lamb, the redemption of the nations, the new creation, the end of tears. It is honey. And the prophetic task of declaring that gospel — to peoples, nations, languages, kings who may not want to hear it — is bitter: it involves suffering, rejection, the cost of witness, the grief of watching the world refuse what is offered. Every faithful preacher knows both at once. The sweetness does not dissolve the bitterness; the bitterness does not cancel the sweetness. John is told: you must prophesy again. Again. The commissioning is renewed precisely because the task is hard.

11.title: The Two Witnesses and the Seventh Trumpet
11.overview:
Chapter 11 is the most compressed chapter in Revelation, covering the entire church age from two angles: the measuring of the temple (the church’s preservation), the ministry of the two witnesses (the church’s prophetic witness), their death and resurrection (the church’s apparent defeat and vindication), and the seventh trumpet (the declaration of the kingdom consummated). It is also one of the most contested chapters in the book.

The measuring of the temple in vv. 1–2 has generated enormous debate. Dispensationalists understand it as a prophecy of a literal rebuilt temple in Jerusalem during the tribulation, the outer court given over to Gentile domination for 42 months. The amillennial reading understands the temple as the church (following Paul’s regular use of temple-language for the believing community — 1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:21; 2 Corinthians 6:16) and the measuring as God’s preservation of his people. The outer court “given over to the nations” represents the church’s visible vulnerability to worldly power — it will be trampled — while the inner sanctuary (the true community of the redeemed) is preserved.

The two witnesses of vv. 3–13 are the most important image in the chapter. Their identity has been debated endlessly: Moses and Elijah (because of the specific powers: turning water to blood = Moses, shutting the sky = Elijah), Elijah and Enoch (the two who did not die), or — the majority Reformed reading — the whole witnessing church across the church age. The number two is the number of legal testimony (Deuteronomy 17:6; 19:15; Matthew 18:16); the two witnesses represent the complete testimony of the church to the gospel of Jesus Christ. Their supernatural powers (fire from their mouths, power over rain and waters) are the powers of the prophetic word: proclamation that both judges and saves.

The seventh trumpet of vv. 15–19 does not release a new woe but sounds the final declaration of the kingdom: “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever.” This is the answer to the Lord’s Prayer (“Your kingdom come”) and the goal toward which all of history moves. The kingdom is announced as already accomplished — the aorist tense of the verb (“has become”) indicates a completed action. What will still unfold in chapters 12–22 is the working out of what has already been declared from the throne.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
John is given a measuring rod and told to measure the temple of God, the altar, and those who worship there — but not the outer court. The measuring is a sign of preservation (Zechariah 2:1– 5; Ezekiel 40–43, where measuring signals God’s claiming of the space). The outer court is given to the nations for 42 months. The 42 months — also expressed as 1,260 days (v. 3) and “a time, times, and half a time” (12:14) — is the symbolic duration of the church age, drawn from Daniel’s “half seven” (Daniel 7:25; 9:27; 12:7). Three and a half years is exactly half of seven — the number of completeness. The church age is the incomplete half, the time between the two comings, the time of testing and tribulation that precedes the full consummation.

The two witnesses prophesy for 1,260 days clothed in sackcloth — the garment of lamentation and repentance, like Elijah on Carmel and John the Baptist in the wilderness. Their testimony is urgent, costly, and counter-cultural. They are described as the two olive trees and the two lampstands standing before the Lord of the earth — imagery from Zechariah 4, where the two olive trees supplied oil to the lampstand, representing the Spirit’s empowerment of God’s witnesses (Zechariah 4:6: “not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit”). The church’s witness is not a human achievement; it is Spirit-empowered testimony that flows from the inexhaustible supply of the anointing.

After completing their testimony, the beast from the abyss makes war on them and kills them. Their bodies lie in the street of “the great city that is symbolically called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified.” The great city is Jerusalem in the immediate reference — it is where Jesus was crucified — but it is called Sodom (for its wickedness) and Egypt (for its slavery and idolatry), transforming it into the symbol of every city and every civilization that opposes the witness of Christ. The world celebrates the witnesses’ deaths for three and a half days, sending gifts to one another in their glee.

After three and a half days, the breath of life from God enters them, they stand up, terror seizes those who see them, and a loud voice from heaven says “Come up here!” — and they ascend to heaven in a cloud while their enemies watch. An earthquake kills seven thousand; the rest are terrified and give glory to God. The pattern is unmistakable: the death, resurrection, and ascension of the two witnesses mirrors the death, resurrection, and ascension of their Lord. The church that is killed for its witness participates in the pattern of the one whose witness it sustains.
verseByVerse.theology:
The death, resurrection, and vindication of the two witnesses is the pattern of all faithful witness. The church does not overcome by winning on the world’s terms — by accumulating political power, cultural credibility, or social influence. It overcomes by being faithful to the point of death and being vindicated by the God who raises the dead. This is the theology of the cross applied to the church’s mission: the apparent defeat of faithful witness is not the end of the story. Three and a half days after the world celebrates, the witnesses stand up.

The great city being symbolically called Sodom and Egypt even though it is “where their Lord was crucified” is a theological claim of permanent importance: the city of God becomes the city of the world when it rejects the testimony of God’s witnesses. Jerusalem is not exempt from the judgment that fell on Sodom and Egypt simply because the temple stands there. Presence of the institutions of religion does not equal the presence of God. This judgment applies to the church in every age.
verseByVerse.examples:
The three and a half days of the witnesses’ unburied bodies — the world celebrating, exchanging gifts, gloating over the silencing of the prophetic word — is the experience of the church whenever it has been apparently crushed. The Reformation was “dead” for seasons. The Chinese church appeared “dead” after 1949. The Ugandan church appeared “dead” under Idi Amin. In every case, after three and a half days, breath returned. The witnesses stood up. The celebration of the enemies was premature.

The two witnesses in sackcloth are not a triumphalist church claiming political power and cultural dominance. They are a prophetic church, urgent in witness, costly in faithfulness, willing to be silenced and to rise. The church that is comfortable and celebrated is probably not in sackcloth. The church in sackcloth may be the most faithful church of the age.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I was given a measuring rod like a staff, and I was told, "Rise and measure the temple of God and the altar and those who worship there, but do not measure the court outside the temple; leave that out, for it is given over to the nations, and they will trample the holy city for forty-two months."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The measuring of the temple echoes Ezekiel 40–43 (the measuring of the restored temple as a sign of God’s renewed presence) and Zechariah 2:1–5 (the measuring of Jerusalem, where God himself is the protective wall). To measure is to claim, to assess, to protect. God is declaring: this community is mine; I have measured it; I know exactly what it is and where it is; I am preserving it.

The outer court given to the nations for 42 months is the church’s visible vulnerability. The outer court of the Jerusalem temple was accessible to Gentiles; only Jews could enter the inner courts. In the spiritual reading, the outer court represents the church’s visible life in the world — its institutions, its buildings, its social standing — all of which are subject to worldly power and can be trampled. The inner sanctuary — the true worshipping community before God, the souls of the redeemed — is preserved. The world can destroy the visible church; it cannot destroy the church that God has measured.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will grant authority to my two witnesses, and they will prophesy for 1,260 days, clothed in sackcloth. These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands that stand before the Lord of the earth. And if anyone would harm them, fire pours from their mouth and consumes their foes. If anyone would harm them, this is how he is doomed to be killed. They have the power to shut the sky, that no rain may fall during the days of their prophesying, and they have power over the waters to turn them into blood and to strike the earth with every kind of plague, as often as they desire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The witnesses prophesy “clothed in sackcloth” — not in triumph and glory but in lamentation, urgency, and the garment of repentance-preaching. Elijah wore a garment of hair (2 Kings 1:8); John the Baptist wore camel’s hair and a leather belt (Matthew 3:4). The prophetic ministry is not a comfortable ministry; it calls the world to repentance, which the world does not appreciate.

The two olive trees and two lampstands from Zechariah 4 represent Spirit-empowered witness. In Zechariah’s vision, the two olive trees supply the lampstand with oil continuously — the Spirit without measure. The church’s witness is not dependent on human eloquence, political access, or social acceptability. It is dependent on the one who says “not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit” (Zechariah 4:6). The fire from the witnesses’ mouths is the word of God as judgment (Jeremiah 5:14: “I am making my words in your mouth a fire, and this people wood, and the fire shall consume them”). The word that saves those who receive it judges those who reject it.

And who are the two witnesses? Readers have long divided, and the text pulls two ways. The miracles point to individuals: shutting the sky recalls Elijah (1 Kgs. 17:1), and turning water to blood and striking the earth with plagues recalls Moses (Ex. 7–12) — which is why some expect two end-time prophets, often named as Moses and Elijah, or Enoch and Elijah (the two men in Scripture who never died). Yet John calls them “two lampstands,” and lampstands, he has just told us, are churches (1:20); “two” is also the number Scripture requires for valid testimony (Deut. 19:15). So others read them as the whole witnessing church. Either way, the emphasis falls where the passage does: their God-given message, their divine protection until the work is done, and their share in their Lord’s death and vindication.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they have finished their testimony, the beast that rises from the bottomless pit will make war on them and conquer them and kill them, and their dead bodies will lie in the street of the great city that symbolically is called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified. For three and a half days some from the peoples and tribes and languages and nations will gaze at their dead bodies and refuse to let them be placed in a tomb, and those who dwell on the earth will rejoice over them and make merry and exchange presents, because these two prophets had been a torment to those who dwell on the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The beast from the abyss makes its first appearance here — it will be described more fully in chapter 13. The timing is precise: the witnesses are killed “when they have finished their testimony.” Not before. They are invulnerable while their prophetic task continues; only when that task is complete does God permit their death. This is the sovereignty of God over the martyrdom of his witnesses: no one can silence the church before it has said what God appointed it to say.

The refusal of burial is the ultimate insult in the ancient world — it left the dead without honor and without the hope of proper passage to the afterlife in the surrounding culture. The gloating of the “those who dwell on the earth” — Revelation’s consistent phrase for those whose ultimate orientation is toward earthly things rather than the kingdom of God — reveals the true depth of the world’s hostility to the prophetic word. The prophets were “a torment” to them: not because the prophets were cruel but because truthful witness torments those who are determined to live in a comfortable lie.

One line rewards a careful reader: the bodies lie in “the great city that symbolically is called Sodom and Egypt, where also their Lord was crucified.” The city where the Lord was crucified is Jerusalem — yet John will not simply name it, because it is behaving like the world at its worst. He calls it Sodom (the byword for moral corruption, Gen. 19) and Egypt (the byword for enslaving God’s people, Ex. 1–14). The point is character, not geography: wherever God’s witnesses are put to death, that place — even a holy city — has thrown in its lot with Sodom, Egypt, and the crucifiers. “The great city” becomes Revelation’s name for the whole world in its rebellion against God (cf. 17:18).

verseByVerse.quote: But after the three and a half days a breath of life from God entered them, and they stood up on their feet, and great fear fell on those who saw them. Then they heard a loud voice from heaven saying to them, "Come up here!" And they went up to heaven in a cloud, and their enemies watched them. And at that hour there was a great earthquake, and a tenth of the city fell. Seven thousand people were killed in the earthquake, and the rest were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven. The second woe has passed; behold, the third woe is soon to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The breath of life from God entering the witnesses echoes Ezekiel 37:10, where the breath of God entered the dry bones and they stood on their feet — the resurrection of Israel from the death of exile. The pattern is unmistakable: death, resurrection, ascension. The witnesses mirror their Lord in the pattern of their defeat and vindication. The “Come up here!” echoes 4:1, where the same words summoned John into the heavenly vision — but here it is the vindication of the martyred witnesses before the eyes of their enemies.

The earthquake and the falling of a tenth of the city and the death of seven thousand produce terror — and “the rest were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven.” Whether this “glory to God” represents genuine repentance or merely terrified acknowledgment (as in 6:16, where the kings call on the mountains to fall on them) is contested. The Greek allows either reading. The context of chapter 9’s non-repentance suggests the latter — but the interlude of chapter 11 may be designed to offer a note of eschatological hope: even from the ruins of judgment, some come to give God glory.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The seventh trumpet does not release a further woe upon the earth. It releases instead the final declaration of the kingdom. Loud voices in heaven cry: “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever.” The twenty-four elders fall on their faces and worship. The temple in heaven is opened, and the ark of the covenant appears within it, accompanied by lightning, rumblings, thunder, an earthquake, and heavy hail.

This is the climax of the trumpet series and, in a sense, of the whole book. Everything that follows in chapters 12–22 is the unpacking, the elaboration, the showing of what this declaration means. The kingdom has come. Christ reigns. The nations are angry; God’s wrath has come; the time for judging the dead and rewarding the saints and destroying those who destroy the earth has arrived. All of this is stated as accomplished fact at the seventh trumpet, even though the bowls and the final judgments remain. The pattern is the same as the Lamb taking the scroll in chapter 5: the authority is declared in heaven before it is fully executed on earth.

The opening of the temple and the appearance of the ark of the covenant is the culminating revelation of the chapter. The ark — which disappeared from history after the Babylonian destruction of the temple in 586 BC, its fate unknown — is revealed in the heavenly temple. It was never lost. It was never destroyed. It was in the heavenly sanctuary all along, where Moses’ earthly tabernacle was only “a copy and shadow” (Hebrews 8:5). The ark is the throne of God’s presence, the place of atonement, the heart of the covenant. Its appearance signals: the covenant has been kept. God has been faithful. The promises stand.
verseByVerse.theology:
The declaration “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ” is the fulfillment of Daniel 2:44 (the stone that becomes a great mountain filling the whole earth) and Daniel 7:14 (the Son of Man given dominion, glory, and a kingdom that shall not pass away). It is also the fulfillment of the Lord’s Prayer: “Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven.” The kingdom for which the church has prayed across twenty centuries is declared a reality at the seventh trumpet. From the throne’s perspective, it is done. From earth’s perspective, the working out continues.

The wrath of God that has “come” (v. 18 — again the aorist, completed action) alongside the rewarding of the saints and the judging of the nations is the two-sided verdict of the final judgment: the wicked face God’s wrath; the righteous receive the reward of the kingdom. Both are expressions of the same justice. The reward of the saints is not a sentimental addition to the judgment of the wicked — it is the flip side of the same verdict: God declares what is true and gives to each what is due.
verseByVerse.examples:
The seventh trumpet is the basis for the church’s confidence in prayer and witness. When we pray “Your kingdom come,” we are praying into something that has already been declared from the throne. The kingdom is not a project the church is building from the ground up; it is a reality that the Lamb has already established and that the church is proclaiming and living into. This does not eliminate the urgency of mission; it grounds it in certainty rather than anxious effort.

The appearance of the ark of the covenant in the heavenly temple is the assurance that no covenant promise has been lost. Everything God promised Abraham, everything God promised David, everything God promised through the prophets — it is all preserved in the heavenly sanctuary, all intact, all still in force. The apparent losses of history — the temple burned, the ark gone, the covenant people scattered — are provisional. The heavenly reality has never wavered.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the seventh angel blew his trumpet, and there were loud voices in heaven, saying, "The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever." And the twenty-four elders who sit on their thrones before God fell on their faces and worshiped God, saying, "We give thanks to you, Lord God Almighty, who is and who was, for you have taken your great power and begun to reign."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The loud voices (plural — a great choir of heavenly beings) proclaim the kingdom in the past tense: it “has become.” In the prophetic vision, what is certain is declared as accomplished. The kingdom that will be fully manifest at the second coming has been, from God’s eternal perspective, always certain; the declaration at the seventh trumpet is the announcement of its irreversible arrival. “He shall reign forever and ever” — the eternal reign is the counterpoint to every temporal power that has claimed sovereignty over the earth.

The twenty-four elders’ thanksgiving focuses on the fact that God “has taken your great power and begun to reign.” This is not a new development — God has always reigned. It is the eschatological manifestation of that reign in undeniable, universal clarity. The one who has always ruled is now seen to rule by all. The hiddenness of God’s governance that has allowed the wicked to prosper and the righteous to suffer is now dissolved: the kingdom is manifest.

verseByVerse.quote: The nations raged, but your wrath came, and the time for the dead to be judged, and for rewarding your servants, the prophets and saints, and those who fear your name, both small and great, and for destroying those who destroy the earth. Then God's temple in heaven was opened, and the ark of his covenant was seen within his temple. There were flashes of lightning, rumblings, peals of thunder, an earthquake, and heavy hail.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fourfold action of the seventh trumpet — the nations raging, God’s wrath coming, the dead being judged, and the saints being rewarded — parallels Psalm 2 almost exactly: the nations rage (Psalm 2:1), the LORD laughs and judges (Psalm 2:4–5), the Son receives the nations as his inheritance (Psalm 2:8), and the kings are warned to submit (Psalm 2:10–12). Revelation 11:18 is the fulfilment of Psalm 2. The small and the great are rewarded equally — kingdom status is not determined by earthly prominence.

The ark of the covenant appearing in the heavenly temple is the culminating revelation. The earthly ark was the footstool of God’s throne, the place where the blood of atonement was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement, the container of the law that the people had broken. In heaven, the ark is intact, the covenant is unbroken, the atonement is complete. The lightning and thunder and earthquake and hail that accompany its appearance echo the Sinai theophany (Exodus 19:16–19) — the giving of the law is here shown to have its heavenly completion in the keeping of every covenant promise that the law pointed toward.

12.title: The Woman, the Dragon, and the War in Heaven
12.overview:
Chapter 12 is the theological heart of Revelation. Everything that has come before — the seals, the trumpets, the witnesses — and everything that follows — the beasts, the bowls, Babylon’s fall — is explained here. We are shown the cosmic backstory: the war between the dragon and the woman, the birth of the child who will rule all nations, the war in heaven that cast Satan down, and the dragon’s fury against the woman’s offspring. This is the explanation for why the church is persecuted: the dragon, having failed to destroy the child, turns his fury on those who “hold to the testimony of Jesus.”

The great sign in heaven — the woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet and a crown of twelve stars — draws on Genesis 37:9 (Joseph’s dream where the sun, moon, and eleven stars bowed down to him, representing his family) and on the Old Testament imagery of Israel as the bride/mother of God’s people (Isaiah 54; Jeremiah 6:2). The woman is not Mary (though the imagery encompasses the incarnation). She is the messianic community — Israel who gave birth to the Messiah, and the church who is the continuation and expansion of that community. She is clothed with cosmic glory; she is in labor.

The great red dragon with seven heads and ten horns and seven diadems is Satan himself, identified explicitly in v. 9: “that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world.” His seven heads and ten horns anticipate the beast of chapter 13, which mirrors the dragon’s appearance — the beast is the dragon’s instrument, Rome as the embodiment of satanic opposition to Christ. The dragon’s tail sweeping down a third of the stars has been interpreted as the fall of the angels who followed Satan in the primordial rebellion.

The cosmic war of vv. 7–12 is one of the most dramatic scenes in Revelation: Michael and his angels fight the dragon and his angels; the dragon is thrown down. The war in heaven is won. The announcement that follows is the theological explanation: they conquered “by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death.” The cross — not Michael’s sword — is the decisive weapon. The dragon is thrown down because the Lamb was slain.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Woman and the Dragon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The vision opens with two great signs: the woman clothed with the sun (v. 1) and the great red dragon (v. 3). The contrast is deliberately cosmic in scale. The woman bears the glory of the entire created order — sun, moon, stars. The dragon is “great” and “red” (the color of bloodshed and destruction) with seven heads (complete worldly power), ten horns (the fullness of kingship), and seven diadems (“crowns” — but the Greek is diadēmata, the royal crowns of kings, not the victor’s crowns stephanoi of the overcomers). The dragon’s crowns are royal and worldly; the woman’s crown of twelve stars is cosmic and covenantal.

The woman is in labor, crying out in birth pain. The dragon stands before her, ready to devour the child the moment he is born. This is the cosmic interpretation of what was happening in Bethlehem: behind Herod’s massacre of the innocents, behind Caesar’s census that drove Mary and Joseph to Bethlehem, behind the entire history of satanic opposition to the messianic line — the dragon waiting to devour the child. The birth of Jesus is not a private event in a Judean village; it is the crisis moment of the cosmic war.
